#30. UK poised to miss reduced aid spending target of 0.3% of national income

Calculations from the Center for Global Development say spending next year is likely to be £410m less than anticipated

The UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on international aid by an estimated £400m by the end of next year.

Calculations from the Center for Global Development (CGD) found the UK was on course for a large shortfall in promised official development assistance at the end of 2027.

The researchers said the central forecast from the Treasury’s comparison of independent experts implied UK aid would be £410m less than anticipated – at only 0.29% of national income.

However, they said it was “very plausible” that the shortfall would be £580m, at only 0.28% of national income. Even the most conservative forecast implies a £250m shortfall, according to the estimates.

Ian Mitchell, a senior fellow at the CGD and co-director of its Europe programme, described these as “material shortfalls in the spending power of UK aid”.

Making up a shortfall of even £400m would be enough to halve cuts to Africa that are likely to cost thousands of lives and mean the UK’s de facto exit from the south and east of the continent, he said.

The CGD attributed the shortfall to higher than expected inflation, which means national income will be higher than forecast at the spending review, and a 2025 policy change around the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) budget.

The researchers called on ministers to consider allocating additional funds to international aid in this week’s budget, to avoid the embarrassment and criticism from missing a target.

The 0.3% spending target for 2027 is far below the 0.7% promised in Labour’s election manifesto, having been downgraded by Keir Starmer to boost spending on defence.

Fleur Anderson, a former minister who sits on the foreign affairs select committee, said she would like to see higher spending on development aid in the budget.

She said: “I’d like to see this government going further and reversing these cuts altogether in time, but at the very least we should be hitting the reduced target that was set.

“Falling short isn’t an abstract accounting issue. It means communities not having clean water, girls pulled out of school, vaccines that don’t get delivered, peace programmes in war zones cut.

“The upcoming budget presents real opportunity for the Treasury to address this and for the government to show that its words on Britain’s place in the world are matched by action.”

Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters

Charities have repeatedly said that the government’s deep aid cuts will hit children’s education and increase the risk of disease and death in some African countries.

The latest figures released by the FCDO in September showed that British aid cuts under Starmer’s government hit the world’s poorest countries the hardest, while higher-income countries’ share of aid increased. The data showed a 6.7% decrease in funding to the least-developed and low-income countries, amounting to cuts of £118m.

The UK’s overall official development assistance (ODA) budget in 2025 decreased to 0.44% of gross national income, compared with 0.5% in 2024, a drop of £987m.

The government has prioritised spending through multilateral agencies such as the World Bank’s development arm, the International Development Association, and the global vaccines initiative Gavi. It has also continued to fund humanitarian support.

The Conservative party and Reform UK have pledged to slash aid even further, from about £9bn a year to £1bn – a level that would leave the UK unable to cover existing contributions to the UN and World Bank.

An FCDO spokesperson said: “The publication of the FCDO multi-year ODA allocations in March 2026 set out our spending plans and priorities for the next three financial years based on GNI [gross national income] at the time of the 2025 spending review.

“Moving to a fixed budget reduces volatility and provides the necessary stability to deliver high-impact aid programmes.”

#32. Polri Ajak Masyarakat Saring Informasi dan Bijak Bermedia Sosial

Polri mengajak masyarakat untuk menyampaikan aspirasi secara damai dan bertanggung jawab, serta bijak menyikapi informasi yang beredar di media sosial.

Kebebasan berpendapat ditegaskan sebagai bagian penting dari demokrasi yang harus dihormati, dengan tetap memperhatikan hak orang lain dan ketertiban umum.

Kadiv Humas Polri Irjen Pol. Johnny Eddizon Isir mengatakan, hak menyampaikan pendapat di muka umum dijamin dalam Undang-Undang Nomor 9 Tahun 1998 tentang Kemerdekaan Menyampaikan Pendapat di Muka Umum.

Namun, pelaksanaannya juga disertai kewajiban untuk menghormati hak dan kebebasan orang lain, menaati hukum, serta menjaga ketertiban umum.

"Polri menghormati hak masyarakat untuk menyampaikan kritik dan aspirasi. Kami mengajak masyarakat menggunakan hak tersebut secara bijak dan bertanggung jawab. Perbedaan pendapat merupakan bagian dari demokrasi, dan dapat disampaikan secara tegas tanpa harus mengabaikan hak orang lain maupun ketertiban bersama," ujar Johnny dalam keterangannya di Jakarta, Selasa (27/10).

Ia juga mengingatkan masyarakat agar lebih cermat menerima dan menyebarkan informasi di ruang digital.

Pasalnya, informasi yang tidak utuh, potongan video tanpa konteks, maupun narasi yang belum terverifikasi berpotensi menimbulkan kesalahpahaman apabila langsung dipercaya dan disebarluaskan.

Johnny mendorong masyarakat untuk membiasakan diri memeriksa sumber informasi, memahami konteks, serta merujuk pada sumber tepercaya sebelum menarik kesimpulan.

Menurutnya, media sosial seharusnya menjadi ruang untuk bertukar gagasan dan menyampaikan kritik secara konstruktif, bukan menjadi sarana penyebaran provokasi.

"Pastikan informasi yang kita terima benar sebelum membagikannya. Mari gunakan media sosial secara bertanggung jawab, tetap kritis, dan tidak mudah terprovokasi. Menjaga ruang digital yang sehat merupakan bagian dari tanggung jawab kita bersama," pungkas Johnnya.

Polri mengajak seluruh elemen masyarakat untuk terus menjaga ruang demokrasi yang terbuka, damai, dan saling menghormati.

Dengan memahami hak dan kewajiban dalam menyampaikan pendapat serta bijak menggunakan media sosial, masyarakat akan dapat berkontribusi menjaga persatuan dan menciptakan kehidupan bermasyarakat yang aman dan kondusif.

#34. Kalah dari Borneo FC, pelatih PSS Sleman sesalkan kartu merah

Yogyakarta (ANTARA) - Pelatih PSS Sleman Pieter Huistra menyesalkan kartu merah yang diterima salah satu pemainnya saat menghadapi Borneo FC Samarinda pada pekan ketujuh Super League 2026/2027 di Stadion Internasional Maguwoharjo, Kabupaten Sleman, Daerah Istimewa Yogyakarta (DIY), Selasa.

"Kartu merah itu adalah hal yang (berpengaruh) besar dalam pertandingan," kata Huistra dalam konferensi pers usai pertandingan.

Kartu merah tersebut diterima Stefan Ashkovski pada menit ke-43 setelah melakukan pelanggaran terhadap pemain Borneo FC di area pertahanan, sehingga PSS Sleman harus melanjutkan pertandingan dengan 10 pemain.

Menurut Huistra, kehilangan satu pemain akibat kartu merah sangat memengaruhi permainan dan strategi tim.

"Kami harus bertahan lebih baik, dan setelah kartu merah, saya pikir keseluruhan dinamika dalam game berubah," ujarnya.

Meski menghadapi situasi sulit, Huistra menilai para pemainnya tetap berjuang dan tidak menyerah hingga mampu memperkecil ketertinggalan melalui satu gol.

"Para pemain tidak menyerah. Bahkan saat tertinggal 1-0 dan bermain dengan 10 orang, kami mencoba untuk melawan, kami mencoba mengambil risiko, kami menciptakan beberapa peluang, dan pada akhirnya kalah 1-2. Sedikit kurang beruntung," katanya.

Baca juga: Borneo FC tumbangkan PSS Sleman 2-1 di Maguwoharjo

Huistra memahami kekalahan tersebut mengecewakan suporter, pemain, dan staf tim, tetapi ia menilai permainan kedua tim relatif berimbang.

"Saya mengerti suporter, mereka sangat kecewa, para pemain juga kecewa, staf juga kecewa. Kalau Anda lihat ke game, ya saya pikir kedua tim kurang lebih setimbang," ujarnya.

Sementara itu, pemain PSS Sleman Riko Simanjuntak mewakili rekan-rekannya menyampaikan permohonan maaf kepada seluruh suporter atas kekalahan dari Borneo FC.

"Saya mewakili pemain, tentunya memohon maaf kepada semua suporter yang telah hadir, yang enggak hadir juga, atas hasil ini. Tentunya hasil malam ini bukanlah hasil yang kami inginkan," katanya.

Riko mengatakan seluruh pemain berkomitmen untuk berusaha mengamankan tiga poin dalam setiap laga kandang, tetapi target tersebut belum dapat diwujudkan saat menghadapi Borneo FC.

"Semua bisa melihat Borneo juga punya kualitas, dan kita tadi dari awal sudah memberikan perlawanan dan kita beberapa menciptakan peluang juga, dan Borneo juga demikian," ujarnya.

Ia menambahkan, kartu merah tersebut membuat pelatih melakukan perubahan strategi yang berisiko bagi PSS Sleman, tetapi para pemain tetap berusaha menjalankan instruksi di lapangan.

"Saat ada kartu merah pasti ada yang perubahan, dan pelatih juga di locker room membuat perubahan yang tadi juga sudah ngomong itu berisiko, ternyata luar biasa juga, teman-teman berjuang," katanya.

#37. Can Black voting power and Trump fatigue break Mississippi's red wall?

Mississippi Democratic Senate nominee Scott Colom speaks at a rally in Columbus, Miss., headlined by former Vice President Kamala Harris on Oct. 22, 2026. Stephen Fowler/NPR hide caption

COLUMBUS, Miss. — On paper, Mississippi's U.S. Senate race seems like the perfect place for a political upset this year, an assertion President Trump's Monday rally there seems to support.

It has the highest share of Black voters in the country, at close to 40%. It's a rural, agriculture-heavy state that is also among the poorest, so higher prices are felt harder.

But President Trump won the state by 23 points in 2024, and it's extremely racially polarized, meaning not enough white voters back Democrats for the party to win statewide.

In a midterm environment that has seen hundreds of millions of dollars poured into Senate races in conservative-heavy states like Iowa, Texas, Ohio and Alaska, and a last-minute flood of cash to Kansas, the Magnolia state has been left off of many peoples' radar — and largely out of campaign investments.

Scott Colom, a district attorney and the Democratic Senate nominee in Mississippi, told NPR that's a mistake.

"The reality is, Mississippi has never been a lost cause, we've been a betrayed cause," he said. "The Democratic Party has not been trying to win Mississippi. Let's stop kidding ourselves, right? They spent hundreds of millions of dollars in other states. They spent almost nothing in Mississippi."

Colom is challenging incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith, who blocked his nomination to be a federal judge during the Biden administration.

In the final weeks of the election, both parties have rushed to spend millions of dollars in Mississippi, as national polling shows a pathway where Democratic enthusiasm and elevated Black turnout, combined with fewer Republican base voters and defections from the party, has made deep red races deeply competitive this cycle.

The crowd listens during a rally with former Vice President Kamala Harris and Mississippi's Democratic Senate nominee Scott Colom in Columbus, Miss., on Oct. 22. Stephen Fowler/NPR hide caption

At a rally for Colom in his hometown high school gym Thursday, about a thousand people showed up to hear the candidate — joined by former Vice President Kamala Harris — give his closing message.

Many attendees expressed optimism for his campaign coupled with a vibe of feeling down about those in power, regardless of party affiliation – citing the war in Iran, rising fuel costs and dissatisfaction with Trump's second term.

That includes Celestine Rice, who said many people were realizing a need to focus on bringing change to the political system and representation.

"Before, we didn't realize how bad it was, but now it's obvious," she said. "The moral compass of this country is gone."

Rice said many people took for granted an era where it seemed the country used to be more focused on taking care of its citizens and now they see that "big money, it doesn't trickle down like they said."

The brunt of the Democratic money and manpower headed to Mississippi is driven by a growing number of those who argue the party's future runs through the South, including Harris, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock and former transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg.

At the rally, Harris said political changes in the last year and a half were the result of "the most callous, corrupt and incompetent presidential administration we have ever experienced."

"We've been going through that range of emotions from anger to sadness to depression, all of that for a year and a half," she said. "Well guess what? We're 12 days out from an election. And it's time to turn that anger into action."

President Trump embraces Mississippi Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith at a campaign rally on Oct. 26, 2026 in Corinth, Miss. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images hide caption

About a hundred miles up the road a few days later, Trump, Hyde-Smith and other Mississippi Republicans gathered in Corinth to motivate the party's base to show up and vote next Tuesday.

In a statement ahead of the rally, Hyde-Smith's campaign manager expressed confidence in her reelection bid.

"We are confident that Mississippians will once again send Cindy Hyde-Smith to the U.S. Senate," Jake Monssen said. "Senator Hyde-Smith and President Trump have built a strong working relationship, and she gladly accepted when President Trump offered to help rally voters and support her get-out-the-vote efforts.

"With so much at stake in this election, Mississippians deserve to hear directly from their President about the consequences of electing Democrats, the radical socialist policies being pushed by Scott Colom, and the importance of this election. Team Cindy looks forward to a successful, high-energy event in Corinth," he said.

Speaking ahead of the president, Hyde-Smith touted accomplishments from her time in office and said the choice facing voters "could not be clearer."

"We know what we're looking at: this is socialism versus capitalism, and we know that," she said. "Communism versus democracy, and big government versus the free market. It could not be higher stakes."

Hyde-Smith repeatedly reiterated that it was important for Republicans to get out and vote.

"Endorsements don't win elections, votes win elections," she said.

Mississippi Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith talks to audience members as President Trump holds a campaign rally in support of her reelection campaign on Oct. 26, 2026 in Corinth, Miss. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images hide caption

For his part, Trump said his visit to Mississippi was because Hyde-Smith was in good shape in her matchup.

"Sometimes when you think somebody's doing so well, nobody votes," Trump said. "'Oh, Cindy's great, she's gonna do no problem, let's stay home.' And then bad things happen, Cindy. That's why I'm here, just get out and vote."

Over the last month, the Republican campaign strategy has been to highlight the investment and attention from national Democrats as proof Colom is too extreme for Mississippi — and have spent heavily on ads saying as much.

"Meet the most radical Senate candidate in our lifetime, Scott Colom," an ad titled "Most Radical" intones. "Twice nominated by Biden, beholden to the far left. As DA, violent crime doubled on his watch."

The Hyde-Smith campaign has spent more than $1.3 million on that ad, according to data from AdImpact.

But Democrats have spent more this month, about $5 million to the Republicans' $3.2 million, with a message that there's no daylight between the unpopular president and down ballot Republicans.

"I mean, the reality is if somebody's doing a good job, it's hard to beat them," he said. "If Cindy Hyde-Smith was focused on the voters, it'd be tough. But it's very clear the voters of Mississippi want to fire her."

The race carries weight beyond Mississippi, or even control of the Senate. It's become a stand in for conversations about the power of Black voters in the South.

Many Southern Republican-led states have rushed to redraw Congressional maps that remove opportunities for Black voters to elect candidates of their choice after a Supreme Court ruling earlier this year rolled back part of the Voting Rights Act.

In Mississippi, Republicans have signaled a desire to redraw state legislative and judicial races after the midterms, and Colom said it could extend even further into local elections.

"What that tells us is you're trying to take away power from the voters and give it to the leaders," he said. "That's not how democracy is supposed to work. The voters have to pick the leaders, not the leaders pick the voters.

In a statewide race that can't be gerrymandered, and in an environment favorable to Democrats, history and math still prove to be a challenge. The last Democratic Senator from Mississippi came in the early 80s. The last successful Black statewide candidate was during Reconstruction.

Even during the 2018 blue wave, Cindy Hyde-Smith won a special election for this seat by roughly 7 points.

Still, there are many factors that have both parties anxiously awaiting results on Nov. 3, including a pervasive anti-incumbent streak that has shown up in polls and primaries this election cycle coupled with a significant increase in Black voter turnout in states that have early voting.

Ashley Kennedy Shelton, who runs a nonpartisan civic engagement group in Louisiana, told NPR earlier this month that people of all stripes have been expressing frustration and a desire for change.

"I think you're going to see voters truly show up, because folks are just tired," she said. "They're like: 'This doesn't work, and it hasn't been working for quite some time.' I think you're going to see it at the ballot box.

NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

#39. Databricks co-founder shares his secrets for winning big enterprise customers

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

Startups have never been under more pressure to grow quickly. To do that, many of them must land large enterprises, the deep pockets of the IT world, as customers. But as any company that sells to enterprises will tell you, it’s not easy to win such contracts.

One critical mistake most younger startups make is believing that their tech will practically sell itself, says Arsalan Tavakoli-Shiraji, co-founder and senior vice president of field engineering at Databricks, which helps businesses store and analyze huge amounts of data.

Yes. The tech must work well. But that’s not enough, he warns. Databricks today is an AI and big data storage giant, valued at $190 billion, with more than 70% of the Fortune 500 as customers. But it was once a tiny startup, and Tavakoli-Shiraji was responsible for helping bring in its first big deals.

“Everybody when they’re selling to enterprises at startups … we think it’s all about the tech and having the best tech,” Tavakoli-Shiraji told attendees at TechCrunch Disrupt last week. But he learned the hard way that “people and processes matter the most.”

He remembers securing a meeting with a prospect in the early days, only to discover that it was the same person who signed a mega-deal with his major competitor. “He has no interest in listening to me because he bet his career on that competitor,” Tavakoli-Shiraji said. He also remembers early deals fizzling because the startup wasn’t prepared for legal, contractual, or security questions.

He offered his top tips for startups to win big customers:

When Databricks was young, it tried and failed to score a meeting with UBS, the large Swiss bank. Then it did “a partnership with Microsoft,” becoming an Azure cloud partner. That meant sales agreements would be covered under Microsoft’s terms.

But it also meant that Microsoft’s sales folks actually booked the meetings and advocated for the startup. “All of a sudden, that meeting wasn’t hard to get,” the founder recalled. “It was a huge boon to us that we were able to partner with somebody who had that access and distribution.”

With Microsoft’s sales team helping, “we started getting pulled everywhere.” That created new problems, like prospects wanting features for countries Databricks hadn’t expanded to, but they were good problems to have.

Today, Databricks is the big company that works with startups, selling their products under Databricks’ own terms and cybersecurity setup. Examples include Hightouch, which provides AI-powered marketing and customer-data tools (Databricks has also invested in it); Addepar, which offers data tools for investment professionals; and Tecton, a machine learning startup that Databricks later acquired.

Tavakoli-Shiraji groups enterprises’ main concerns and objections into four categories he calls the four Cs: context, choice, cost, and control. Context means an AI that can be trained “like bringing on a new employee,” he says, learning the company’s terminology, processes, priorities, and so on.

Choice is the freedom to switch AI models rather than be tied to a single provider. Cost is about controlling how much the AI product will cost to run. Control involves the safeguards that govern the AI’s behavior and protecting sensitive information.

Tavakoli-Shiraji jokingly asks CIOs where they stand with AI on a scale of one to five. A one means employees merely have access to ChatGPT, and a five means the company has adopted new AI capabilities that have changed its business processes.

“And everybody loves picking, ‘I’m three leaning towards four.’ But 99% of the ones I talk to are in bucket one and two.” Enterprises still haven’t figured out how to deploy AI agents in ways that create value beyond allowing engineering teams to write code. “It’s going to take many, many years before people can actually properly deploy AI in a very meaningful way in the enterprise.”

One big opportunity for startups to bring that value is to modernize expensive legacy systems. “If you go to any bank today, they still have [an IBM] AS/400 and mainframes,” he described. “Nobody wanted to touch it because nobody knew what that code did.”

But today, AI agents “can go in and understand and actually decompose what that code does.” That, he says, opens the door to products that do everything from adding modern interfaces for those ancient systems to replacing them altogether.

Tavakoli-Shiraji also shared his predictions for the future of enterprise AI adoption, along with an anecdote of what happened when the company was young and he pretended to be a lawyer to land a big enterprise contract. See the full interview below.

#40. Mystery over source of Ebola infection in Nigeria fuels concern about spread of virus

Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda

Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.

The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.

The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.

The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no ​Ebola cases and that, if ​it did, it would make that information ​public.

The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.

Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video ‌link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.

Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, ​but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.

Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same ​space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”

The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.

Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.

“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.

Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.

Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

Sinetron ini dibintangi oleh Salsabila Andriani (Sera Maharani), Jefri Nichol (Kenzi Adrian), Marvin Daneswara (Arya Vasco), Rachel Patricia (Clara Putri), Benny Ruswandi (Prayoga Bratanegara), Cinta Dewi (Lena Saputri) dan aktor-aktris berbakat lainnya.

Kenzi dan Bebeto memulai hidup baru di kontrakan sederhana bersama Lena dan Alea. Dengan uang pas-pasan, mereka berusaha menyiapkan hadiah ulang tahun untuk Lena. Bebeto menawar harga mukena, sementara sandal dibayar menggunakan QRIS. Meski Lena sedih karena Kenzi meninggalkan dunia tinju, kebersamaan mereka perlahan menghangatkan suasana.

Bimo kemudian menawarkan diri dan menghajar lawannya saat sparring. Ia bahkan menyindir Marvin soal Bram, sementara Prayoga membebankan kesiapan Bimo kepada Marvin.

Di tengah usaha membangun kehidupan baru, Kenzi mulai mencemaskan kondisi Lena. Saat mengimami salat, ia melihat setetes darah dari hidung sang ibu jatuh ke mukena. Wajah Lena yang pucat membuatnya curiga, terlebih Alea kemudian mengungkapkan bahwa Lena harus segera menjalani transfusi darah.

Jika menunggu jadwal BPJS, prosesnya bisa terlalu lama, sedangkan biaya pengobatan secara mandiri diperkirakan mencapai Rp6,2 juta. Kenzi menangis karena merasa tak berdaya menghadapi kebutuhan tersebut. Harapannya untuk mengandalkan uang Bebeto pun pupus setelah saldo yang tampak mencapai Rp1 juta ternyata berkaitan dengan utang pinjaman online. Mereka juga tidak jadi menjual tablet sekolah Alea maupun motor peninggalan ayahnya, Si Buyung. Meski demikian, Kenzi tetap berjanji akan mendapatkan uang yang dibutuhkan.

Sementara itu, Sera kembali dihantui trauma masa lalunya di penjara. Dalam mimpi buruknya, ia terlibat perkelahian dengan narapidana yang merebut jatah ayam hingga harus dikurung di sel isolasi. Sera terbangun dalam keadaan ketakutan, seolah pengalaman pahit itu belum benar-benar meninggalkannya. Di tengah kondisi yang belum pulih, ia juga sedang menganggur dan memasang status “open for work” di LinkedIn. Bersama Lita, Sera pergi ke pasar dan belajar menawar belanjaan. Tak disangka, sebuah pesan langsung dari Lena berisi undangan ulang tahun beserta lokasi kontrakan baru membuat Sera kembali berhadapan dengan masa lalu yang belum selesai.

Sera awalnya berniat mengabaikan undangan tersebut. Namun, Lena memergokinya di pasar dan mengungkapkan bahwa ia sudah mencari Sera melalui berbagai akun media sosial, bahkan membaca kutipan tentang karma yang diunggah Sera. Situasi semakin canggung ketika Lita keceplosan bahwa Sera baru saja dipecat. Meski begitu, Lena kembali mengundangnya dan meminta Kenzi menyiapkan wadah untuk membawa pulang makanan. Sera akhirnya mengiyakan undangan itu, sementara Kenzi hanya bisa memandangnya dengan khawatir.

Polda Metro Jaya meminta seluruh elemen masyarakat untuk bersama-sama menjaga fasilitas umum dan ruang publik saat demo pada Rabu (28/10).

Kepolisian juga menekankan pentingnya saling menghormati dan menjaga ketertiban agar masyarakat dapat menyampaikan pendapat dengan aman dan damai, sementara aktivitas warga lainnya tetap berjalan dengan baik.

Kabid Humas Polda Metro Jaya Kombes Budi Hermanto mengatakan ruang publik merupakan tempat bersama yang digunakan masyarakat untuk berbagai kepentingan, termasuk menyampaikan aspirasi, bekerja, bersekolah, dan menjalankan aktivitas sehari-hari. Karena itu, seluruh pihak diharapkan saling menjaga dan menghormati hak masing-masing.

"Ruang publik adalah milik kita bersama. Ada masyarakat yang menyampaikan aspirasi, ada pula yang bekerja, bersekolah, dan menjalankan aktivitas sehari-hari. Semua memiliki hak yang perlu kita hormati," kata Budi dalam keterangan tertulis, Selasa (27/10).

Budi menerangkan menjaga fasilitas umum merupakan bagian dari tanggung jawab bersama karena keberadaannya berkaitan langsung dengan kebutuhan masyarakat.

Kata dia, komunikasi yang terbuka dan penyampaian informasi yang akurat juga penting untuk mencegah kesalahpahaman serta menjaga situasi tetap aman dan kondusif.

Hal tersebut sejalan dengan semangat 'Polisi Bersama Masyarakat untuk Saling Menjaga Ruang Publik sebagai Sarana Penyampaian Pendapat', yang menekankan pentingnya penghormatan terhadap hak warga, keselamatan, dan kepentingan bersama.

"Aspirasi masyarakat harus tetap mendapat ruang, sementara keselamatan dan kepentingan bersama juga kita jaga. Inilah semangat Polisi Bersama Masyarakat dalam menjaga Jakarta," ucap dia.

Sangatta, Kaltim (ANTARA) - Badan Pemeriksa Keuangan (BPK) RI Perwakilan Provinsi Kalimantan Timur memperdalam hasil pemeriksaan sebelumnya tentang izin usaha tambang, sekaligus mengonfirmasi sejumlah temuan tentang kepatuhan penyelenggaraan perlindungan, pengelolaan lingkungan dan kehutanan.

Pendalaman hasil pemeriksaan tersebut dibahas dalam audiensi Tim BPK RI Perwakilan Provinsi Kalimantan Timur (Kaltim) bersama Bupati Kutai Timur Ardiansyah Sulaiman di ruang kerja bupati, di Sangatta, Selasa (27/10).

Dia menambahkan koordinasi dengan pemerintah daerah menjadi bagian penting dalam proses tersebut, terutama untuk memperoleh penjelasan dan data yang dibutuhkan sesuai dengan kewenangan masing-masing perangkat daerah.Sementara, Bupati Kutai Timur Ardiansyah Sulaiman, meminta seluruh perangkat daerah terkait memberikan dukungan kepada tim pemeriksa, termasuk melalui penyediaan data, dokumen, dan keterangan yang diperlukan dalam proses pemeriksaan.

#44. Media groups challenge India’s privacy law at top court

News organisations are challenging the law, arguing it could hamper investigative journalism and endanger sources.

The Indian government’s privacy law, which would require journalists to seek consent from people they write about, amounts to pre-censorship and could lead to newsrooms shutting down, media groups have told the Supreme Court.

A group of 21 news publishers, including companies owned by billionaires Mukesh Ambani and Gautam Adani, challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s law on Tuesday, arguing it would trample upon investigative work and allow the government to identify journalists’ sources, according to The Indian Express newspaper.

“It is changing the whole concept of what is news,” Madhavi Goradia Divan, the lawyer for the Digital News Publishers Association (DNPA), told judges.

“Newsrooms will shut down, if we have to ask for permission … it’s then a complete regime of pre-censorship.”

The Supreme Court said it would hear the case next month.

Media companies received assurances in an August meeting with the government that the law would protect press freedom, but not having a written exemption for journalists as in the European Union, Singapore and Britain was alarming, the news publishers said in a filing earlier this month.

The DNPA’s members include Ambani’s Network18, which has seven digital news platforms, Adani’s NDTV and other high-profile media groups including the Indian Express and Times Internet, which is part of the Times of India group, publisher of India’s largest-selling English-language daily.

A key concern in the law is the requirement of consent, says the group’s filing, cited by the Reuters news agency.

A social media platform or online retailer can seek consent from users when they sign up, but the DNPA has argued that requiring a journalist to notify the subject of an investigation and seek consent “would allow that subject to destroy evidence, intimidate witnesses”.

The law also lets people withdraw consent at any time and demand that their data be erased, without any public-interest safeguard, which the DNPA says could force its members to unpublish or heavily redact a factual news report.

News publishers are concerned that a federal authority created under the law can impose fines for noncompliance, and grants powers to New Delhi to block access to any information in the “interests of the general public”, which would curtail press freedom, the DNPA said.

From next year, the law will also let New Delhi order any organisation handling personal data “to furnish such information as it may call for”, putting newsrooms at risk of having to divulge sources, the filing said.

It can also deter whistleblowers from sharing information on corruption, corporate wrongdoing or electoral malpractice with reporters, the DNPA argued.

The “nakedly unguided” provision must be quashed, the DNPA said, adding that the power “can extend to privileged communications in possession of a reporter or the informant.”

#48. Watch out, YouTube — Instagram goes from short-form to 90-minute videos

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

If you could have 1 million followers on any social media platform, which would you choose? There is a correct answer, and it’s YouTube, assuming you’d like to get paid for your work. But Instagram’s latest update could upend YouTube’s long-held position as the most lucrative platform for creators, if only Instagram plays its cards right.

Instagram announced on Monday that it’s testing a new type of video upload that will allow creators to share “Features,” videos up to 90 minutes long. After years in which every social platform (even LinkedIn!) aggressively pursued short-form video, this is a notable shift in strategy for Instagram.

Short-form, vertical video content has defined the internet of the 2020s, but the creators behind these clips don’t actually make much money directly from platforms like Instagram — the Meta-owned platform has some monetization tools like subscriptions, but it doesn’t typically pay creators on a per-view basis.

“You can get paid by the platform directly, you can get paid by a fan, and you can get paid by a brand,” Instagram head Adam Mosseri explained on the Colin and Samir Show, an interview show about the creator economy. “And right now, the way that it works on Instagram primarily is you primarily get paid by brands. Some people get paid by fans. We have still a small performance-based program, but … we spend more money than we make back by a long shot, and so it doesn’t really make sense to scale up because we’re just burning capital.”

YouTube’s payment model is more straightforward: There are ads on videos, and creators enrolled in YouTube’s Partner Program get 55% of the ad revenue YouTube earns from their videos. That adds up. The platform said last year that it paid more than $100 billion to creators, artists, and media companies in the previous four years.

Instagram and TikTok haven’t been able to replicate YouTube’s model with short-form content, which is inherently trickier to monetize than longer videos because there’s less room to place ads. Many creators see those accounts more like promotional arms for their YouTube channels than meaningful drivers of revenue.

Instagram is encouraging creators to upload longer videos, as it already did eight years ago with the now-defunct IGTV. It’s possible that its parent company, Meta, which makes its billions on advertising, will put ads in those long-form videos, too.

If Meta does add ads, could Instagram meaningfully compete with the YouTube Partner Program for the first time?

“It’s too early to share a long-term monetization model, but we’re exploring ways for creators to earn from brands, fans, and Instagram, including performance-based incentives,” a Meta spokesperson told TechCrunch. “Over time, we think there will be compounding benefits for creators to tell new stories, reach new audiences, and find new partners, which should lead to many monetization opportunities.”

It’s not a particularly promising answer, but it’s also not a no.

Mosseri explained in a video announcement why the platform is suddenly embracing long-form content after scrapping its old video product, IGTV.

“For a long time, I have been against doing long-form video on Instagram,” Mosseri said, noting that shorter content like Reels drives more shares and DMs among users. Instagram VP of Product Tessa Lyons, who has been advocating for this change, finally convinced Mosseri to give long form another shot.

“Reels is still going to be a core part of Instagram. But when you want to go deeper with the creators you love and the content that they’re creating, you should be able to do that on Instagram,” Lyons said in the video.

In other words, Instagram would rather keep fans on its own platform to enjoy both short- and long-form content from a creator than lose them to YouTube. Instagram is testing a feature called “Clips as Reels,” which lets creators make Reels out of their long-form content. The Reels link viewers to the longer video. Viewers can also save the longer video to send to the Instagram app on their TV.

Instagram is currently testing “Features” and “Clips as Reels” in Brazil and will now expand to the U.S. in a small test. The platform is also working on improved discovery features for Live video and a hub on a creator’s profile for episodic Reels, meaning a series of connected Reels similar to TikTok’s playlist feature.

“The thing that the team has been working on that we’re excited to share with you is trying to make it so that the short-form and the long-form video can be symbiotic,” Mosseri said. “We’re going to try to support these different types of formats, both in the mobile app, but also on the TV app, which I think is … going to take some time to get right. But I’m actually very excited about it, and we’re very committed to it long term.”

#49. Democrats still poised to make gains, but poll shows warning signs for just how many

A member of the League of Women Voters of Greater Cleveland helps hold the flag during the national anthem before a basketball game on Oct. 26, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. Jason Miller/Getty Images hide caption

📲 Get the latest on the midterms & more in the NPR App

Democrats retain significant midterm electoral advantages, with key data pointing to them being the favorites to win control of the U.S. House. But, there are indications of why a potential wave could be limited, a new NPR/PBS News/Marist poll finds.

The poll also sheds light on the issues driving voters across the ideological spectrum. The cost of living continues to be top of mind overall with a third of people saying they've experienced financial hardship in the past year and 4 in 10 saying their personal finances have gotten worse.

"The economy is at the top of my list right now," said Shun Maurice, a 47-year-old from Arizona who participated in the poll. He's an independent who leans toward Democrats and said high food and gas prices are a strain.

"They're too expensive for everybody, no matter who you voted for," he said. "They're just too expensive for the American people in general, and I don't like that."

Preserving democracy also continues to resonate with Democrats and independents, while immigration is the biggest concern for self-described MAGA supporters.

The poll of 1,289 registered voters was conducted Oct. 19-20. When registered voters are mentioned, the margin of error is +/- 3.7 percentage points. When likely voters are mentioned, it is +/- 3.8 points.

This was the first survey this cycle that Marist applied a likely voter screen, and on multiple questions, likely voters were — within the margin of error — slightly less likely than registered voters to disapprove of the president. Likely voters overall were also slightly less likely to want Democrats to run Congress.

Likely voters are something of a special sauce in polling. Survey researchers apply various metrics — like levels of enthusiasm, past voting history and how important voting is to different respondents — to try to identify the subsample of people who are most likely to vote.

In this survey, just 38% of registered voters approved of the job President Trump is doing, with 61% disapproving (-23). Likely voters gave him a 40% to 59% rating (-19), still not very good, but even a slight margin can make a difference in how significant the gains either party might make in the election are.

That said, an equal share — 53% — of registered and likely voters said they "strongly disapprove" of the job Trump is doing, tied with last month as the highest ever in the poll.

Trump's favorability rating is even lower — just 37% of likely voters have a favorable impression of Trump, while 59% have a negative one.

Democrats also had a strong advantage on which party's candidate people said they are more likely to vote for in their district if the election were held today, known as the generic congressional ballot. Among registered voters, it was a 10-point advantage. With likely voters, it was 8 points, still indicative of Democratic gains.

When Democrats have had that kind of lead on the congressional ballot, they have historically done very well. On average, it was +7 in 2018 and +12 in 2006. In both years, Democrats won the House with at least 30 seats flipped.

But that was before the 2020 Census and ensuing regular redistricting — and the rare, mid-decade redistricting in the last year and a half after Trump asked Republican states to redraw their maps to potentially give Republicans more seats. Though Democrats followed suit, both redistricting periods have tilted congressional seats in Republicans' direction and given them a relative advantage nationally.

Perhaps because of some of those structural disadvantages and past performance, there is a notable degree of nervousness among Democrats.

While 98% of Democratic likely voters said they would vote for a Democrat, just 81% thought the Democrat would win, a 17-point difference. Republicans were only 10 points less likely to believe their candidate would win. Notably, among independents, a higher share thought the Democratic candidate would win.

Working in Democrats' favor — and against incumbents: 55% of likely voters said it's more important in this election to vote for candidates with new ideas who will bring about change. (It was a tick higher with registered voters at 57%.)

Chris Agan, a 43-year-old Democrat in Tyler, Texas, who participated in the survey, never saw himself as an impassioned midterm voter, until this year.

"This year is different. This year, it feels like every opportunity to vote is a referendum against the party in power," said Agan, who's backing Democrat James Talarico over Republican Ken Paxton in the race for U.S. Senate.

"We've been seeing a very slow decline in the standard of living in this state, and it's becoming apparently evident to more people at this time," he added. "I think Talarico embodies that realization that there needs to be change."

Double the percentage of likely voters also said their vote would be one against Trump (44%) as opposed to one for him (21%). In the 2024 presidential election, 55% of those who voted for Trump said their vote was for their candidate, according to exit polls.

Trump is not on the ballot, but he has asked voters to "pretend" he is.

Though Trump's unpopularity poses challenges for Republicans, it may not directly translate to more votes for Democrats. Some swing voters don't like the lurch in some corners of the Democratic Party toward democratic socialism.

Matthew Schroder is a 38-year-old independent living in Charlotte, N.C., who was part of the poll. He backed Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump in 2024. Now, he says that while he's unhappy with Trump's job performance, it isn't what's driving his vote this year.

"What I have seen on the left-hand side is a little bit more of an embrace of democratic socialism, which I just oppose completely," said Schroder, who's supporting Republican Michael Whatley over Democrat Roy Cooper in the state's closely watched race for U.S. Senate.

"I know Roy Cooper is considered a moderate, but the fact that the Democratic Party is even letting some of these voices be heard a little bit more … is not something I'm interested in in the least," he added. "It's not a vote of 'yes for Trump' as much as a vote of, Democrats need to completely reject [democratic socialism] and go a completely different direction."

Democratic likely voters are 10 points more likely to say they are "very enthusiastic" about voting (71% vs. 61%). That's actually wider than the difference between Democratic and Republican registered voters in the poll.

The caution for Democrats, though, is that several of their key pillar groups are not very enthusiastic to vote, and Republicans have closed the gap on who is following the election "very closely."

Just 42% of likely voters under 45, 53% of non-white voters and 56% of white women with college degrees said they are "very enthusiastic" to vote. All of those groups disapproved of the job Trump is doing.

Compare that to pro-Trump groups — MAGA voters (68%), white women without degrees (66%) and white evangelical voters (61%).

For independents, 48% report being very enthusiastic to vote.

Traditionally, younger, as well as Black and Latino voters turn out at disproportionately lower rates in midterm elections. But with the realignment under Trump, more white, college-educated voters are voting Democratic and, as a group, they turn out at the highest rates.

When it comes to paying close attention, last month just 34% of registered Republicans said they're following the election very closely, compared to 42% of Democrats.

Now, they're even – 46% of Democrats and 45% of Republicans said they're paying very close attention. When it comes to likely voters, there's no difference either – 51% of Democrats to 50% of Republicans.

On the positive side for Democrats: those who voted for Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024 are 15 points more likely than Trump 2024 voters to say they are very enthusiastic. And Democrats overall have an 8-point advantage over Republicans when it comes to who cares a "great deal" about who controls Congress.

Three-quarters of likely voters are confident that their state and local governments will run a fair and accurate election.

That includes solid majorities of Democrats (88%), Republicans (68%) and independents (75%), but Republicans were 20 points less likely than Democrats to think they would be run well. MAGA supporters were almost 30 points less likely.

Large majorities also said their preferred candidate should accept the results of the election. That included 70% of Republicans, but again, they were 20 points less likely than Democrats to say they should accept the results. A quarter of Republicans said their candidate should probably or definitely challenge the results.

There was also a sharp divide between those who identified as democratic socialists and MAGA supporters — 86% of democratic socialists but only 65% of MAGA supporters said their preferred candidate should accept the result. MAGA supporters were twice as likely to say they should challenge.

Methodology: This NPR/PBS News/Marist Poll was conducted from Oct. 19-20 and surveyed a national sample of 1,289 registered voters. They were reached through a multi-mode design: by phone, text or online. To create a likely voter sample, Marist applied a likely voter weight to all registered voters. When registered voters are mentioned, the margin of error is +/- 3.7 percentage points. When likely voters are mentioned, it is +/- 3.8 points. That means results fall within a range of roughly eight points – about four points lower or higher.

#50. Hari Pertama Operasi Patuh, 103.779 Pelanggar Lalu Lintas Ditindak Lewat E-TLE

JAKARTA — Direktorat Lalu Lintas (Ditlantas) Polda Metro Jaya mencatat 103.779 pelanggaran lalu lintas yang terekam melalui sistem tilang elektronik atau Electronic Traffic Law Enforcement (E-TLE) pada hari pertama Operasi Patuh Jaya 2026, Senin 26 Oktober 2026.

Kasubdit Gakkum Ditlantas Polda Metro Jaya, AKBP Muhammad Adiel Aristo, belum merinci wilayah maupun jenis pelanggaran yang dilakukan para pengendara. Namun, sebanyak 2.888 pelanggaran telah tervalidasi dan surat pemberitahuan penindakan telah dikirimkan kepada pelanggar.

“Kendaraan yang telah terkonfirmasi ada sebanyak 1.872 dan tertagih 1.976,” ujarnya, Selasa (27/10/2026).

Menurut Adiel, sebanyak 1.777 pelanggar telah membayar denda. Sebagai informasi, Operasi Patuh Jaya 2026 digelar selama 14 hari, mulai 26 Oktober hingga 8 November 2026. Dalam operasi tersebut, Polda Metro Jaya mengerahkan 2.938 personel gabungan.

Operasi Patuh Jaya 2026 mengusung tema 'Polisi Bersama Masyarakat Mewujudkan Lalu Lintas yang Tertib, Aman, dan Berkeselamatan'. Adiel menyebut keselamatan lalu lintas harus diwujudkan bersama oleh petugas kepolisian dan masyarakat.

Sejumlah pelanggaran menjadi sasaran operasi tersebut, di antaranya pengendara sepeda motor yang tidak menggunakan helm berstandar SNI dan pengemudi mobil yang tidak mengenakan sabuk pengaman. Pelanggaran lainnya meliputi penggunaan ponsel saat berkendara, pelanggaran rambu atau marka jalan, menerobos lampu merah, melebihi batas kecepatan, melawan arus, serta mengangkut muatan secara berlebihan.

#51. Reader Q&A: After Lula’s sensational victory in Brazil’s presidential election, post your questions for the Guardian’s Latin America correspondent

Having lost the first round of Brazil’s presidential election to far right rival Flávio Bolsonaro, incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva spectacularly triumphed in the second. What comes next for Brazil? The Guardian’s Tom Phillips will be answering your questions from 15:00 GMT today.

Ask a question: log in or sign up here to comment, or email conversations@theguardian.com

After losing the first round of Brazil’s presidential election to far right rival Flávio Bolsonaro, incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, better known simply as Lula, pulled off the most stunning political fightback in modern Brazilian history by winning the second, in so doing securing a fourth presidential term. It will see him become the country’s longest-serving leader.

The result – 51.79% to Lula, 48.21% to Bolsonaro – was delivered after a supreme court judge had extended polling time by two hours, and after Lula’s camp accused their opponents of sabotaging public transport in an attempt to keep their voters from the polls. It was the first time in Brazilian electoral history that a first-round verdict had been overturned.

But Bolsonaro, son of former president Jair Bolsonaro who is serving a 27-year jail term for his part in an attempted coup after the last presidential election, refused to accept the result – just as his father had done, four years before. He called Lula’s victory “sacanagem”, a Portuguese word that roughly translates as “bullshit”.

Brazil remains a deeply divided country and Lula will have to navigate a hostile Congress, packed full of Bolsonaro allies, if he is to make significant legislative changes in his fourth term. His options are also constrained by a gloomy economic outlook, with Brazil experiencing soaring debt and entrenched structural problems. As he turns 81, will the re-elected president have the energy to face down the far right opposition for another four years and to lay out the ground for a credible successor?

And what does Lula’s latest victory mean for the wider region, and for the country’s relationship with Donald Trump’s administration? In the Guardian’s Opinion pages columnist Jordana Timerman wrote that “Lula’s victory shows that the rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible. But the movement retains substantial electoral support, influence over the political agenda and a powerful ally in Washington.”

The Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips will be answering your questions on the election result, what it means for Brazil and the wider region, and what the country’s future may hold, here from 15:00 GMT on Tuesday 27 October. Comment with your question below, or email conversations@theguardian.com

#52. SKK Migas sebut UEA akan kirim 30 juta barel minyak mentah ke RI

Jakarta (ANTARA) - Kepala Satuan Kerja Khusus Pelaksana Kegiatan Usaha Hulu Minyak dan Gas Bumi (SKK Migas) Djoko Siswanto mengungkapkan bahwa Indonesia akan mendapatkan pasokan minyak mentah hingga 30 juta barel dari Uni Emirat Arab (UEA).

Djoko mengatakan pembahasan mengenai pasokan minyak tersebut menjadi salah satu hal yang disampaikan saat dirinya mendampingi Menteri Energi dan Sumber Daya Mineral (ESDM) Bahlil Lahadalia menerima Duta Besar UEA di Jakarta, Selasa.

"Duta Besar Abu Dhabi menyampaikan akan mengirim minyaknya ke Indonesia sampai dengan 30 juta barel tanpa biaya, tanpa working capital, termasuk free kapalnya. Ini suatu kabar yang bagus juga buat kita," katanya dalam acara "Penyelesaian Front-end Engineering Design/FEED Proyek LNG Abadi Masela" di Jakarta, Selasa.

Namun, Djoko tidak merinci skema kerja sama dan mekanisme pasokan tersebut, termasuk pembiayaan, jadwal pengiriman, serta cakupan pembebasan biayanya.

Selain membahas importasi minyak mentah, Djoko menyampaikan bahwa pertemuan tersebut juga membahas progres keputusan investasi akhir atau final investment decision (FID) proyek gas di Blok Andaman, wilayah lepas pantai Aceh.

Pemerintah sebelumnya menyatakan akan memperkuat ketahanan energi nasional melalui penjajakan pasokan dari sejumlah negara.

Menteri ESDM Bahlil Lahadalia dijadwalkan melakukan kunjungan ke India dan China untuk memperoleh kepastian pasokan, sementara PT Pertamina ditugaskan mencari kontrak pasokan jangka panjang.

Upaya tersebut juga sejalan dengan perubahan mekanisme pengadaan energi impor melalui Peraturan Presiden Nomor 107 Tahun 2026.

Kebijakan tersebut mengatur pengadaan minyak mentah, bahan bakar minyak (BBM), dan liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) melalui kerja sama langsung antarpemerintah (government-to-government/G2G) maupun pemerintah dengan badan usaha (government-to-business/G2B).

Melalui skema tersebut, pemerintah menegosiasikan pengadaan dengan negara pemasok, sementara badan layanan umum (BLU), yang ditugaskan pemerintah melaksanakan pengadaan, memasoknya kepada Pertamina.

Kebijakan itu ditujukan untuk memperkuat kepastian pasokan energi dalam negeri di tengah ketergantungan Indonesia terhadap impor, terutama untuk minyak mentah dan LPG.

#53. Polri Dorong Penyampaian Aspirasi Damai untuk Jaga Ruang Demokrasi

Kepolisian Negara Republik Indonesia (Polri) mengajak seluruh elemen masyarakat untuk menyampaikan aspirasi secara damai, tertib, dan bertanggung jawab. Kebebasan berpendapat dinilai sebagai hak setiap warga negara yang perlu dihormati, sekaligus dijalankan dengan mengedepankan kepentingan bersama.

Masyarakat diimbau tetap menghormati hak sesama saat menyuarakan pandangan di ruang publik. Perbedaan pandangan serta kritik dipandang sebagai bagian penting dari keberlangsungan demokrasi yang sehat.

Kepala Divisi Humas Polri, Irjen Pol. Johnny Eddizon Isir, mengimbau masyarakat agar tidak ragu menyampaikan aspirasi secara konstruktif. Ia juga meminati warga tidak mudah terprovokasi oleh informasi yang belum terverifikasi kebenarannya.

"Polri menghormati setiap aspirasi masyarakat. Kritik dan perbedaan pendapat merupakan bagian dari demokrasi. Mari sampaikan aspirasi secara damai, jaga ruang publik bersama, dan jangan mudah terprovokasi," ujarnya dalam keterangan tertulis, Selasa (27/10).

Ia menegaskan bahwa Polri mengedepankan pelayanan humanis melalui komunikasi dan pendekatan persuasif. Pendekatan itu bertujuan agar masyarakat dapat menyampaikan pendapat dengan baik.

Partisipasi masyarakat juga dibutuhkan untuk menjaga ketertiban, menghormati sesama, serta memastikan hak setiap warga tetap terpenuhi.

Johnny turut mengingatkan masyarakat agar bijak bermedia sosial dengan memeriksa kebenaran informasi sebelum menyebarkannya. Informasi yang belum terverifikasi diminta tidak ditanggapi secara berlebihan.

Menurutnya, ruang demokrasi harus dijaga bersama, baik di dunia nyata maupun digital. Hal itu dilakukan agar perbedaan pandangan tidak berkembang menjadi kesalahpahaman di tengah masyarakat.

"Demokrasi bukan hanya tentang keberanian menyampaikan pendapat, tetapi juga kedewasaan dalam menghormati perbedaan. Polri bersama masyarakat, mari kita jaga agar aspirasi tersampaikan, pelayanan berjalan baik, dan kehidupan bermasyarakat tetap aman serta damai," tutup dia.

#56. Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up

UK prepper stores see massive sales following government campaign

Some retailers have seen a dramatic increase in sales of essential goods after the government called for people to stock up in case of a crisis, according to figures obtained by Newsnight.

The Iceland supermarket chain said it was "clear" consumers had listened to warnings after it saw a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend.

The rise in sales came after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that people should stockpile goods to prepare for an emergency such as a cyber attack or an extreme weather event.

Robert Dyas reported a 160% increase in sales of radios compared with last week, while Maplin said sales had increased by 92% in radios, 284% in torches and 106% in power banks.

The Maplin figures cover the period since the government's announcement last week compared with the same period last month.

"Within hours of the Be Ready announcement we saw people reach for the basics - a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank. Torch sales nearly quadrupled and radio sales almost doubled in three days," said Ollie Marshall, managing director at Maplin.

"These are simple, affordable products that keep a household connected and informed when the power goes out, and it's encouraging to see people taking the advice seriously."

On 22 October, Streeting said that people should ensure they have three litres of water per person per day; tinned goods in the cupboard; baby food; battery powered torches and mobile phone charging packs.

Many of the items cited by Streeting appeared in the list of goods gathered by Newsnight whose sales have shot up.

In response to the increase in retail sales of certain items, the defence secretary told Newsnight: "It's encouraging that people are taking practical steps to be ready. Having a few everyday essentials at home, from tinned food to torches, helps households prepare for disruption, whether that's flooding, power cuts or burst pipes. We can all play our part in making Britain more resilient."

An Iceland spokesperson told the BBC programme: "It's clear consumers have listened to the government's message as we have seen a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend and strong sales of bottled water too. Our supplies of these products remain healthy."

Sales of torches and radio have risen sharply for some UK retailers

Newsnight also spoke to independent retailers who reported a spike in sales of goods highlighted by the defence secretary.

Josh Pringle, from Sgt Prepper's online store, said his sales had increased tenfold: "We were a small outfit on Wednesday. And then the government launched the Be Ready campaign and we couldn't believe what we were seeing â order after order after order. Most of them were for a wind-up radio."

Lincoln Miles, founder of Preppers Shop UK, told Newsnight of a 650% increase in sales after the government announcement. "Everything about off grid seems to be the key of what people are buying for the minute."

#58. Uh-oh, it sounds like the iPhone Duo keeps cracking and users aren’t happy about it

Buy One Founder Summit Ticket, Get a Second for Free. Register now.

Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.

The launch of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s hotly anticipated foldable phone, is off to a rough start. The phone was announced at this year’s Surprise and Shine event, with Apple promising that it had finally gotten a notoriously tricky form factor right.

Now, however, Bloomberg reports that early Duo users have been complaining about screens cracking “after just hours or days of use.” Some users have reported hearing a loud crunching noise, followed by the appearance of a crack. Others have reported display malfunctions.

404 Media has also reported that early adopters are dealing with “big fat creases down the middle of the [$2,000] folding screen.”

TechCrunch reached out to Apple for comment and will update this story if it responds. The company told Bloomberg that it was “aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units.”

Creating a functional foldable phone has long been an ambition in Silicon Valley, but many of the models released so far have suffered from similar maladies. Apple promised that it had cracked the code, but these early complaints suggest it may not have solved the problem after all.

#60. Brazil: defeated Flávio Bolsonaro ordered to surrender passports

Far-right senator banned from leaving country as supreme court judge’s ruling makes reference to money-laundering case

The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro was banned from leaving Brazil and ordered to surrender his passports just hours after his dramatic loss in the presidential election to the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The ruling was issued by supreme court justice Alexandre de Moraes, the same justice who oversaw the trial of the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for attempting a coup.

Bolsonaro posted a video saying the decision was based on an interview his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, gave last Friday urging his brother to leave Brazil if he lost the election.

On Monday night, Bolsonaro’s party issued a statement acknowledging the election result, saying: “We recognise the presidential result proclaimed by the electoral court, but believe that the questions raised need to be properly clarified through a balanced and democratic political debate.”

Bolsonaro, like his father four years ago, has still not conceded defeat to Lula.

The court’s brief ruling regarding his passport only refers to a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating Flávio Bolsonaro over his possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme. The ruling orders him not to have any contact with his friend Willer Tomaz, a lawyer linked to betting companies that police suspect were being used to launder about £680m.

It also cancelled all of Bolsonaro’s passports, including the diplomatic one he holds as a congressman, and ordered him to hand them over within 24 hours.

Bolsonaro was the first to speak publicly about the matter, before Brazilian media were even aware of the judge’s decision.

In a video posted on social media, he said he had just left a visit to his father, who is under house arrest in Brasília, when “Lula’s federal police were at his door and in the middle of the street, and I was served with an order to hand over my passports and I am also prohibited from leaving the country”.

He added that, although his brother – who is in self-imposed exile in the US – told a US podcast on Friday that he favoured the senator leaving Brazil if he lost the election, “I never said that”.

When his Senate term ends early next year, Bolsonaro will be out of public office for the first time in 24 years, and therefore without the special jurisdiction afforded to officeholders.

He is under investigation in another criminal case, too, over what happened to the £20m he was captured on tape asking a disgraced banker accused of corruption to provide for a biopic about his father.

The Folha de S.Paulo newspaper reported that Flávio Bolsonaro had been persuaded to drop his plan to seek to annul the election, which he had announced after the result was declared on Sunday night.

Bolsonaro had claimed that the two-hour extension of voting – intended to allow voters who had been unable to access the mandatory free public transport to cast their ballots – had harmed the election, despite the fact that his own campaign had also argued for an extension.

According to the newspaper, allies and lawyers told him his argument was legally weak.

Bolsonaro had still not publicly reversed his demand for an annulment, and in the same video he said he would file another case to have Lula’s ticket disqualified over alleged abuse of economic power, a similar case to others his legal team brought during the campaign.

#64. Nelayan Tewas di Penjara Polsek Kajang, Keluarga Lapor Propam Polri

Keluarga tahanan Anto bin Mallisa Dg Baro melaporkan kasus dugaan penganiayaan hingga tewas yang terjadi di Polsek Kajang, Sulawesi Selatan ke Propam Mabes Polri.

Kuasa hukum keluarga korban, Nidlamu Harby Elghama menyebut laporan tersebut dilakukan lantaran korban Anto diduga dianiaya hingga tewas saat ditahan di Polsek Kajang.

Ia menjelaskan total ada empat orang anggota Polsek Kajang yang dilaporkan lantaran diduga terlibat kasus penganiayaan terhadap Anto.

"Beliau korban, almarhum, wafat di rutan Polsek Kajang. Kita duga kuat terjadi penganiayaan berat," ujarnya kepada wartawan di Mabes Polri, Selasa (27/10).

Harby mengatakan tewasnya korban itu terjadi dalam kurun waktu kurang dari 24 jam sejak korban ditahan di Polsek Kajang pada Selasa (13/10) lalu. Ia menyebut korban juga belum ditetapkan sebagai tersangka dalam kasus pencurian handphone.

"Jangka masa waktu meninggal sekitar kurang lebih 11 jam. Dia berada di Polsek Kajang sejak jam 09.00 (pagi) dan mati wafatnya itu jam 20.00," jelasnya.

Dalam kesempatan yang sama, Kaharuddin selaku saudara dari Anto menjelaskan korban merupakan nelayan yang saat itu telah membeli handphone. Hanya saja, kata dia, korban tidak mengetahui jika handphone yang dibelinya adalah barang curian.

"Korban membeli handphone yang di mana handphone itu tidak diketahuinya adalah handphone curian. Dalam kondisi masih bersandi, korban membawa handphone ini ke konter untuk membuka sandi handphone tersebut," tuturnya.

Saat itu, kata Kaharuddin, pemilik konter yang sedang berupaya membuka sandi handphone yang dibeli Anto tiba-tiba ditelpon oleh seseorang yang mengaku pemilik handphone.

Lantas, saat itu warga beserta pemilik handphone segera membawa Anto ke Polsek Kajang sekira pukul 09.00 WIT. Saat itulah, Anto dijebloskan ke rutan dalam rangka penyelidikan terhadap kasus dugaan pencurian.

"Sehingga pada pukul dari sekitar pukul 13.00, antara pukul 13.00 ke pukul 20.00, di situlah korban mendapatkan penganiayaan berat oleh sejumlah oknum polisi yang bertugas di Polsek Kajang, Kabupaten Bulukumba," jelasnya.

"Maksud dan kedatangan kami hadir di Mabes Polri di Divisi Propam Polri ini adalah supaya penegakan keadilan yang transparansi dan seadil-adilnya buat saudara kami Anto yang telah dilakukan oleh oknum aparat polisi yang bertugas di Polsek Kajang," sambungnya.

Lebih lanjut, Kaharuddin mengatakan pihaknya sengaja melaporkan kasus tersebut ke Propam Mabes Polri karena merasa mendapat intimidasi agar kasus tersebut tidak dilanjutkan dan diselesaikan melalui mediasi.

"Supaya tidak ditekan, ditakut-takuti, dibujuk rayu untuk mencabut laporannya yang sudah dimajukan di Polsek Kajang, dan tidak dibujuk rayu untuk melakukan tindakan perdamaian dengan tujuan supaya terduga pelaku mendapatkan keringanan di persidangan nanti," jelasnya.

Di sisi lain, Kaharudin menyebut total sudah ada empat anggota Polsek Kajang menjalani penempatan khusus (Patsus) dalam rangka pemeriksaan atas kasus tewasnya Anto.

"Dimana saat ini sudah dipatsuskan sejumlah 4 orang seperti yang sudah disebutkan inisialnya tadi, yaitu (Aipda) BA, (Briptu) AA, (Bripka) IE, dan (Aipda) A," ujarnya.

#65. Why Jordan has struck Syria: What we know

Syria says Jordan did not coordinate with Damascus before launching operation in rural Deraa and Suwayda.

Jordan said its air force conducted retaliatory attacks on what it called “dens of terrorist organizations in southern Syria”, linked to suspects accused of being behind last week’s attack on a Greek Orthodox church in the kingdom.

In a post on X, the Jordanian Armed Forces said: “Fighter jets from the Royal Air Force destroyed a number of terrorist sites in southeastern Syria.

“The operation resulted in the killing and wounding of many elements of the terrorist organizations and the destruction of a number of their vehicles,” Jordan’s Armed Forces added.

“The armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with ⁠Damascus.” Jordan’s military said in a further post on X.

ISIL (ISIS) has claimed responsibility for the October 23 church attack.

Jordan did not specify the locations of the attacks or provide casualty figures.

Syria has contradicted Jordan’s account of the overnight attacks.

In a statement, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs informed Jordan of its “complete reservation” over the attacks, which took place “without prior coordination or notification with the Syrian side”.

A Foreign Ministry official told Al Jazeera’s Heidi Pett that the strikes were a “treacherous attack”.

Pett reported from Syria that authorities have said seven people were killed, including three children, in Jordanian air attacks on Deraa and Suwayda countryside.

Syria’s Ministry of Emergency and Disaster Management said its teams had responded to attacks in four sites.

Syria’s civil defence agency said it had recovered the bodies of those killed in attacks. They include five members of one family, including three children and a woman who were killed together in a strike on a tent in the village of al-Taff, in the Lajat area of northeastern Deraa province. Three other members of the family were injured, it said.

In the al-Shayah farms near Nassib, in Deraa countryside, a strike on a farm killed Riyad Karrad, 80. His body was taken to Deraa National Hospital.

In Muzayrib, in the Ein al-Basal area of western Deraa countryside, a strike hit a home. No casualties were reported.

In the town of Shuhayb, in northern Suwayda countryside, a strike on a home killed Mutlaq Abu al-Khail, 60. Rescue teams were still working to recover his body from the rubble when the report was issued.

There was no immediate comment from Jordan on Syria’s accusations that civilians – not armed fighters – were killed.

Shortly after the attacks, Syrian customs authorities on Tuesday closed the Nassib border crossing with Jordan, the only passenger and commercial traffic pathway between the neighbours.

Jordan said its attacks on Syrian territory were in response to an attack on a Greek Orthodox church in Karak governorate.

On Monday, senior government security officials said Jordanian security forces had arrested two brothers and their brother-in-law after a shootout over the violence that killed nine people in a rare attack on the minority Christian community in Jordan on Friday.

Major-General Obaidullah al-Maaytah, Jordan’s director of public security, named the three detained suspects as Hazza Zaidan Mohammed, Meshal Zaidan Mohammed and Ahmad Sami Hussein.

The attack during a funeral prompted Jordan’s King Abdullah II to order security forces to respond with an “iron fist”.

Jordan’s Interior Minister Mazin al-Farrayeh said he was launching an investigation “examining all the circumstances that lead young people towards extremism”.

“The file has not yet been closed; investigations are still ongoing. As of today, there are ⁠no indications of any links between them and other cells,” al-Farrayeh added.

Jordan has conducted multiple air attacks on Syria since 2023, saying it was targeting drug and arms smugglers.

The operations have sometimes hit civilians.

Human Rights Watch demanded accountability after Jordan launched attacks that killed women and children in January 2024.

“Cross-border airstrikes that kill civilians demand scrutiny regardless of the threat posed by drug smuggling from southern Syria,” Human Rights Watch said.

The Jordanian Armed Forces said its operations along its border were aimed at armed groups reportedly carrying narcotics, arms, and explosives that it suspected are linked to Iran-allied groups.

Syria’s Foreign Ministry said it was in contact with Jordan to establish the circumstances of the operation.

Damascus said it will address the aftermath of the attacks while “safeguarding Syria’s security and sovereignty”.

#67. زعيم المعارضة التنزانية يبدأ إضرابا عن الطعام احتجاجا على مراقبة لقاءاته بمحاميه

بدأ توندو ليسو زعيم حزب "تشاديما" المعارض في تنزانيا، أمس الاثنين، إضرابا عن الطعام احتجاجا على القيود المفروضة على لقاءاته الخاصة بمحاميه بسجن أوكونغا في دار السلام، وفق بيان للحزب أوردته مواقع إخبارية تنزانية.

وقال الحزب في بيانه إن 3 من محامي ليسو توجهوا إلى السجن للقائه، لكنهم مُنعوا من الدخول. ودعا السلطات إلى السماح لمحاميه بلقائه دون عوائق لا أساس قانونيا لها، مؤكدا أنه يتابع عن كثب حالة رئيسه.

وكان المستشار القانوني للحزب روغيميليزا نشالا قد أعلن قرار الإضراب بعد زيارة موكله في السجن السبت الماضي. وقال، في حديث للصحفيين نقلته وكالة أسوشيتد برس، إنه حذر ليسو من المخاطر الصحية، لأنه يعتمد على أدوية وكان مستعدا للتوقف عن تناولها. ونقل عنه قوله "أنا مستعد لتحمل العواقب، لكنني سأناضل من أجل سيادة القانون".

قضت المحكمة العليا في تنزانيا، يوم 16 أكتوبر/تشرين الأول الجاري، بأن ضباط السجن كانوا قادرين على التنصت على محادثات ليسو مع محاميه في سجن أوكونغا، وأمرت بتمكين المحامين من لقائه دون أن يُسمع حديثهم، مع السماح للضباط بالمراقبة بالعين، بحسب موقع "إيستلي فويس" (The Eastleigh Voice) الكيني. وذكرت صحيفة "مونانشي" (Mwananchi) التنزانية أن المحكمة أمرت سجن أوكونغا بألا يمنع محامي ليسو من لقائه والتشاور معه على انفراد.

وقال الحزب إن إدارة السجن لم تطبق هذه الشروط. وقال نشالا لصحيفة مونانشي إن إدارة السجون تخرق ذلك الأمر علنا، مضيفا أن ليسو رفض لقاءات يستمع إليها الضباط.

وقال الأمين العام للحزب جون منييكا، بحسب وكالة الصحافة الفرنسية، إن ليسو عبر عن مخاوف "مشروعة" على حياته وسلامته الشخصية بسبب تحدي إدارة السجن للأوامر القضائية علنا، متسائلا عما إذا كان يمكن الوثوق بالطعام الذي يقدمه مسؤولون يخرقون القانون عمدا.

وكان المفوض العام للسجون جيريميا كاتونغو قد قال لصحيفة مونانشي السبت الماضي ردا على شكوى الحزب "سأتابع الأمر مع زملائنا هناك لنعرف ما حدث ومن أين نبدأ لمعالجته". وليس هذا الإضراب الأول لليسو، إذ أضرب عن الطعام في مايو/أيار 2025 احتجاجا على إلزامه بحضور جلسات المحكمة عن بُعد بدل الحضور الشخصي، وفق أسوشيتد برس.

واعتُقل ليسو في 9 أبريل/نيسان 2025 بعد تجمع دعا فيه إلى إصلاحات انتخابية قبل الانتخابات العامة، ووُجهت إليه تهمة الخيانة العظمى اليوم التالي، وهي تهمة قد تصل عقوبتها إلى الإعدام. وتتهمه النيابة بالإدلاء بتصريحات ونشر مواد على الإنترنت بهدف منع إجراء الانتخابات، وهو ما ينفيه، بحسب "إيستلي فويس".

واختتمت المحاكمة في 29 سبتمبر/أيلول الماضي بعد تقديم الادعاء والدفاع مرافعاتهما الختامية، على أن يصدر الحكم في 6 نوفمبر/تشرين الثاني المقبل. ويصف منتقدون، بينهم المعارضة ومنظمات حقوقية، القضية بأنها ذات دوافع سياسية، وفق وكالة الصحافة الفرنسية.

ونجا ليسو (58 عاما) من محاولة اغتيال عام 2017 أصيب فيها بـ16 رصاصة، وعاد إلى تنزانيا عام 2023 بعد سنوات في المنفى، بحسب أسوشيتد برس.

وكان ليسو قد دعا إلى مقاطعة انتخابات أكتوبر/تشرين الأول 2025 ما لم تُجر إصلاحات انتخابية. ومُنع حزبه من المشاركة فيها، وفازت الرئيسة سامية حسن بنسبة 98% من الأصوات، بحسب النتائج الرسمية. كما مُنع مرشحا الرئاسة عن أكبر حزبين معارضين من خوض السباق، مما أشعل احتجاجات وأعمال عنف دامية.

وخلصت لجنة تحقيق عينتها الحكومة، في أبريل/نيسان الماضي، إلى مقتل 518 شخصا على الأقل في 11 إقليما، وقالت إن العدد الفعلي أعلى على الأرجح، لأن بعض العائلات دفنت ذويها دون نقل جثثهم إلى المشارح. ويقدر حزب "تشاديما" عدد القتلى بنحو ألفين، وقالت الأمم المتحدة إنها لم تتمكن من التحقق من هذا الرقم بسبب انعدام الأمن وقطع الإنترنت، وفق أسوشيتد برس.

ووثقت منظمة هيومن رايتس ووتش مقتل 31 شخصا لم يكونوا مشاركين في الاحتجاجات، وتلقت معلومات موثوقة عن 19 حالة أخرى، بحسب "إيستلي فويس".
